title: Recognition of the Internet Federation as Full Member
description: Whether digital sovereignty constitutes recognized territorial control for full membership purposes. The Internet Federation's application was the first membership vote of the Congress and set the philosophical foundation for what 'territory' would mean in international law going forward. Queen Bean's sponsorship was decisive — her argument was that the Congress had been founded to prevent another Chaos Heart Crisis, and the Chaos Heart Crisis had demonstrated that threats did not respect physical borders. Digital infrastructure was infrastructure. Controlling it was sovereignty. The Federation's Digital Plenipotentiary presented documentation of seventeen server arrays, twelve data routing hubs, and a distributed governance network spanning thirty-four existing territories, none of which had objected to the Federation's presence within their borders. The counter-argument, led primarily by Gondor's ambassador, was that territorial sovereignty required exclusive control of defined physical space. A nation that existed inside other nations' territory was not a nation — it was a guest that had decided to vote. The debate ran for six hours across two sessions.
aftermath: Established digital sovereignty as recognized territorial control. The Mushroom Kingdom's abstention was deliberate — Toadsworth the Elder stated in session that the Mushroom Kingdom was not opposed to the Federation's membership but wished to examine the precedent more carefully before endorsing it. This careful abstention was largely ignored by history. The Internet Federation immediately exploited the holographic attendance precedent the vote created, establishing that digital presence constituted physical attendance for quorum purposes. This has caused seventeen procedural arguments in the fourteen years since. Several nations who voted yes have since privately admitted they did not fully understand what they were agreeing to. Several nations who voted no have since built significant economic dependencies on Federation infrastructure and have not discussed their founding vote publicly.
waluigiComment: The right decision made for slightly wrong reasons. Queen Bean understood what she was doing — the Congress needed to establish early that it would not be limited by 19th century definitions of sovereignty, because the problems it was founded to address were not 19th century problems. Gondor's ambassador was not wrong in principle. He was wrong in application. The world already contained digital sovereignty whether the Congress recognized it or not. The question was whether the Congress wanted to have a relationship with that reality or pretend it did not exist. Waluigi voted yes for the same reason he raises his hand when the question matters: because the precedent was correct even when the reasoning was incomplete. Several delegates voted yes because they did not understand what digital territory meant and were embarrassed to ask. Waluigi understood. Waluigi asked anyway. The record shows that Waluigi asked. The record also shows that nobody answered the question Waluigi asked, which was about recursive voting rights when Federation infrastructure processes the votes being cast about the Federation. That question has still not been answered.

title: Dimensional Barrier Monitoring Resolution
description: A framework for systematic monitoring and public reporting of dimensional barrier integrity across all member territories. The Mages Guild's Archmage Delegate presented fourteen years of pre-Congress data on dimensional stress points, barrier thinning events, and the cascade failures that had characterized the Chaos Heart Crisis. The argument was scientific and detailed: the Chaos Heart Crisis had not appeared without warning, it had appeared without monitoring infrastructure capable of aggregating the warnings. Individual nations had noticed local anomalies. Nobody had assembled the full picture. The proposed resolution would establish a standing committee, funded by member contributions proportional to population tier, with permanent staff, standardized reporting protocols, and a public archive of barrier integrity data going back to 1012 BF. The Mages Guild offered to provide the initial technical staff. The Regal Empire objected immediately, arguing that monitoring magical infrastructure over sovereign territory without bilateral consent constituted an invasion of sovereignty. The Progressive Bloc supported the resolution. The Sovereignty Bloc fractured — the Iron Hills supported it, Gondor supported it, but the Regal Empire's Imperial Chancellor applied significant pressure to Sovereignty Bloc members through back-channel conversations that occurred during the lunch recess between sessions.
aftermath: The committee produced exactly three reports before being quietly defunded in 1031 BF when the Regal Empire objected to monitoring over their territory and leveraged Iron Pact economic pressure on wavering members. The three reports that were produced — covering 1026, 1027, and 1028 — documented early-stage dimensional stress in seven locations. One of those locations was the Raventree region. The report noted 'anomalous planar pressure consistent with pre-Crisis stress signatures' and recommended 'continued observation and escalating intervention protocols.' Nobody acted on this recommendation. When the committee was defunded, its archive was transferred to Mages Guild custody. The Raventree Fracture emergency response team is currently working from those three reports and nothing else. Fourteen years of data that would have existed does not exist. The Mages Guild Archmage Delegate's expression during the 1040 emergency session authorization vote was described by three attendees as the most controlled demonstration of grief they had ever witnessed.
waluigiComment: Waluigi supported this enthusiastically and was told to sit down. The problem was not that the resolution failed — it passed. The problem is that passing a resolution and implementing a resolution are different things, and the Congress has never fully understood this distinction. Waluigi raised his hand during the 1031 defunding vote. Waluigi's hand did not count because Waluigi does not have a seat. Waluigi has been raising his hand without a seat for fourteen years and the dimensional fracture does not care about parliamentary procedure. The three reports the committee produced before defunding are now the most important documents in the crisis response. Waluigi read all three of them in 1028. Waluigi raised concerns about the Raventree region anomaly at the 1029 session. Waluigi was told the anomaly was within acceptable parameters. Waluigi asked who had defined the acceptable parameters. Waluigi was told the session was moving to the next item. This is documented in the session minutes for anyone who wishes to look. Waluigi is STILL angry about this. The anger has not diminished with time. If anything it has improved with age the way certain cheeses improve, becoming sharper and more precisely unpleasant.

title: Species Recognition Compact
description: Minimum standards for legal recognition of sapient species across member territories. Champion Alder of the Pokémon League and Elder Yoshi presented jointly, an unusual collaboration that drew immediate attention. The compact established three core provisions: first, that any species recognized as sapient by at least three Congress members must be recognized by all members; second, that recognized sapient species cannot be treated as property, livestock, pest populations, or resources; third, that nations must provide legal recourse mechanisms for sapient species resident within their territory. The drafting process had taken three months of observer consultations before the founding session. The Pokemon League had done most of the technical work. Yoshi's Island provided the political coalition — Elder Yoshi had spent the pre-session period quietly visiting delegations and asking them, personally, face to face, whether they were comfortable with a document that said some kinds of people did not deserve legal protection. Most were not comfortable saying yes to that question when asked directly. The Regal Empire's Imperial Chancellor attempted to introduce an amendment defining sapience by cognitive threshold measurements, which would have excluded several species with non-standard cognition. The amendment failed after the Pokémon League's delegate presented seventeen case studies of Pokemon species with measurable intelligence exceeding the proposed threshold who nonetheless would have been excluded by the measurement methodology. The Regal Empire did not pursue the amendment further at this session.

notable_nay: several Sovereignty Bloc members with contested labor practices

aftermath: The most consequential resolution for ordinary people passed at the founding session. Not perfectly enforced — the Regal Empire's Iron Mandate legislation fourteen years later would directly challenge its provisions — but the legal language it created has been used by advocates in thirty-seven documented cases to protect species that would have had no legal recourse before 1026 BF. The nine no votes were from nations with domestic practices they did not want held to external standards. Several of those nations have since been held to those standards anyway, through bilateral pressure and economic consequences rather than formal Congress enforcement mechanisms. The compact has never been directly enforced through Congress action. It has been enforced through the existence of the standard it created, which gave advocates a reference point that did not previously exist. This is not the same as enforcement. It is better than nothing.
waluigiComment: This is what the Congress is for. Waluigi will defend this resolution against any challenge and has done so three times in procedural contexts since 1026. The compact is not perfect — the threshold debate revealed that some members wanted to draw the line as narrowly as possible and will continue to try — but it created legal language where no legal language existed. Before 1026 BF, a nation could simply decide that a species did not deserve personhood and there was no external framework that said they were wrong. After 1026 BF, there is a framework. It has not always been followed. It has sometimes been actively violated. But it has saved lives that would have been lost without it, and Waluigi can point to specific cases and specific people — specific individuals who exist because this resolution exists. Waluigi keeps a list. The list has names on it. Waluigi does not share the list because some of those individuals live in territories where being named would make them targets. But the list exists and Waluigi knows every name on it. This resolution is worth defending. Waluigi will keep defending it.

title: Trade Route Protections
proposedBy: Iron Hills Dwarven Holds / Beanbean Kingdom (joint)
description: Shared standards for protection of trade routes through multiple member territories, including reduced cross-border tariff friction, mandatory arbitration mechanisms for commercial disputes, and the establishment of the Trans-Doughnut Trade Registry as a permanent administrative body. The Iron Hills delegation had prepared extensively — their documentation included eighteen months of pre-Congress bilateral trade data, a proposed arbitration framework tested against forty-seven historical dispute scenarios, and a complete draft charter for the Trade Registry. Dáin's Representative presented for forty minutes without notes. The proposal was comprehensive enough that most delegates spent the first session reviewing documentation rather than debating. The Beanbean Kingdom's co-sponsorship was political: Queen Bean understood that the Congress needed an early, uncomplicated win, and trade protections were the proposal most likely to achieve genuine consensus. The only substantive debate concerned Registry governance — whether it would be operated by a standing Congress secretariat or function as an independent body. The Iron Hills wanted independence. The Beanbean Kingdom wanted Congress integration. The compromise established the Registry as a semi-autonomous body with a mixed governance board. Both parties were partly satisfied. The proposal passed in a single session, the only founding-era vote to do so.

notable_nay: Two founding members with protectionist domestic trade policies (unrecorded at their request)

aftermath: The Trans-Doughnut Trade Registry is arguably the Congress's most practically successful creation. It processes an average of 340 commercial dispute filings per year, maintains certification records for 12,000 registered trading entities, and has reduced cross-border tariff disputes by approximately 67% compared to pre-Congress bilateral averages. The Registry's governance board has had sixteen contested elections and three constitutional crises of its own. It functions anyway. Rogueport Free City's no vote was later explained by their representative as a principled objection to any mechanism that would require disclosure of trading partner identities. This explanation was accepted at face value by most delegates. The Registry has operated for fourteen years without Rogueport's participation. Rogueport's merchants use the Registry's certification system when dealing with registered counterparties while Rogueport officially maintains that it does not recognize the Registry's authority. This contradiction has never been formally addressed.
waluigiComment: Even Wario's fake representative voted for this one. Waluigi watched 'Mr. W. Wario, Distinguished Plenipotentiary' — who was wearing glasses and a slightly different hat than usual and was unmistakably Wario — raise his hand for the Trade Route Protections with the focused enthusiasm of someone who had done arithmetic about what protected trade routes would do for his income. When everyone can count the coins, cooperation is easy. The Iron Hills deserve credit for coming prepared. Most delegations arrive at Congress sessions with positions. The Iron Hills arrive with documentation. There is a difference between having an opinion about how trade should work and having eighteen months of empirical data about how trade actually works. The Registry operates today because somebody did the boring work of knowing what they were talking about before they opened their mouth. Waluigi has noted this approach. Waluigi has attempted to apply it. The Congress does not always reward preparation. For trade policy, it did.

title: Fawful Condemnation Resolution
description: Formal condemnation of Fawful's aggressive territorial actions, biological warfare through contaminated food distribution, and unauthorized seizure of sovereign military infrastructure across Mushroom Kingdom and Beanbean Kingdom territories. Toadsworth the Elder presented the resolution as a founding-document statement of the Congress's values — that the body would not ignore documented aggression, biological warfare, and sovereignty violations by specific named actors simply because those actors had been defeated before the Congress formally convened. The counter-arguments were procedural: Princess Zelda's Envoy argued that naming specific individuals in founding-era resolutions set a dangerous precedent, that condemnations should address behaviors rather than actors, and that Fawful's current incapacitation made the resolution feel like kicking a defeated enemy rather than establishing principle. Beanbean Kingdom's Queen Bean abstained — unusual given that Beanbean was the co-victim of Fawful's actions — on the grounds that she preferred the Congress's first condemnation be reserved for active ongoing threats. The Mages Guild observer delegation quietly supported the resolution but had no vote. Several Non-Aligned delegates abstained to avoid establishing that the Congress would take sides in bilateral disputes even when one side was clearly the aggressor.
aftermath: The embarrassingly low approval margin — barely simple majority, with the injured party abstaining — undermined the resolution's moral authority before the ink was dry. Multiple delegates who voted no or abstained stated privately that they were not defending Fawful but objecting to the principle of named condemnations. This objection was sincere for some delegates and a convenient excuse for others. Fawful survived condemnation by being alive while the Congress congratulated itself on paperwork. He also survived by being technically incapacitated at the time of the resolution, which meant the condemnation had no practical effect on an actor who was not actively operating. The Congress's first formal condemnation was a statement about the past delivered to no audience. It established no useful precedent. It created no enforcement mechanism. It made the Mushroom Kingdom look like it was asking for validation and not receiving it. Toadsworth the Elder has never proposed a named condemnation again.
waluigiComment: Toadsworth wanted the Congress to say his enemy was bad. The Congress kind of said it, by the thinnest possible margin, with thirteen abstentions. This is not the same as the Congress saying his enemy was bad. This is the Congress saying it was uncomfortable saying anything clearly. Waluigi understands the procedural objections — named condemnations are a tool that gets misused, and the founding members were right to be careful about establishing how it would work. But the way to establish careful use of a tool is to debate the standards for using it, not to abstain until the resolution barely passes and then call that a condemnation. Queen Bean's abstention was the most interesting vote. She was attacked. She chose not to condemn her attacker. She was signaling that she wanted the Congress's first condemnation to mean something when it came. Waluigi agreed with her reasoning. Waluigi voted no on procedural grounds and recorded his reasoning. The records show Waluigi's hand was raised. The records also show Waluigi's hand did not count. These two facts continue to coexist.

title: Observer Status Admissions Batch
description: Admitted twelve factions as non-voting observers in a single batch vote: the Mages Guild (sponsored by Beanbean Kingdom and Pokémon League), Iron Legion (sponsored by Regal Empire), Freelancer Underworld (arrived with forged credentials and was technically admitted before anyone noticed the credentials were forged), Koopa Troop (sponsored reluctantly by Mushroom Kingdom under charter rules regarding parties to unresolved territorial disputes), Team Rocket (appeared, was admitted, and their delegate subsequently could not be located), Rakasha Clans (sponsored by Saddle Arabia), Peach Loyalists (sponsored by Mushroom Kingdom, separately from Koopa Troop sponsorship, creating an unusual situation where Toadsworth sponsored both sides of an unresolved conflict), DK Crew (sponsored by DK Island Territories as a distinct factional interest), Yoshi Clans Coalition (sponsored by Yoshi's Island similarly), Data Merchants (sponsored by Internet Federation), Cybernetic Collectives (sponsored by Internet Federation), and Warioland (self-nominated, sponsorship eventually provided by Diamond City after no other founding member would do it). The batch vote structure was itself controversial — Gondor's ambassador argued each observer application should be considered individually. Queen Bean ruled that individual consideration would consume the entire remaining session time and proposed the batch vote as a procedural accommodation with the understanding that individual review could be requested for any specific admission. Nobody formally requested individual review. The vote proceeded as a batch.

notable_yea: All Iron Pact members on Iron Legion (unanimous)
most Progressive and Sovereignty Bloc members
notable_nay: Three founding members who objected to Freelancer Underworld inclusion
notable_abstain: Kingdom of Gondor (procedural objection to batch process)

aftermath: Most admissions were uncontroversial in retrospect. The Iron Legion's unanimous admission was not uncontroversial at the time — the Pokémon League delegate raised a formal objection about admitting a military organization without civilian governance — but the Iron Pact's bloc voting pressure and the batch format meant the objection was noted and overruled rather than debated. Wario's representative delivered a four-minute speech containing eleven factual inaccuracies about Warioland's economic contributions to regional stability. Waluigi counted the inaccuracies in real time and submitted a written correction to the session record, which was accepted and filed and ignored by everyone except Waluigi. The Freelancer Underworld's forged credentials were discovered three weeks after the session concluded. By that point the admission was procedurally complete. The Congress has never formally addressed this. The Team Rocket delegate who appeared has never been identified. The seat is technically active.
waluigiComment: Waluigi was in the room when the Iron Legion's observer admission came to a vote. Every delegate who might have objected was either allied with the Iron Legion, economically dependent on Regal Empire trade, or had been quietly visited during the lunch recess by someone from the Imperial Chancellor's office. Waluigi had not been visited because Waluigi does not have a seat and therefore cannot be lobbied in the conventional sense. Waluigi objected anyway. Waluigi's objection was noted in the minutes as a procedural comment from an unofficial attendee and carried no weight. The unanimous vote for Iron Legion observer status should have been the first warning that something was being coordinated rather than genuinely agreed upon. When everyone votes yes on something, the question is not whether the outcome is good — the question is who arranged for everyone to agree and what they received in exchange. Waluigi asked this question. Waluigi did not receive an answer. The Iron Legion has been escalating its presence in the Congress ever since 1026. The unanimous founding vote is in the record for anyone who wants to understand how it started. As for Wario's speech — Waluigi sat in the back and counted. Eleven inaccuracies in four minutes is almost impressive. The statement that Warioland had 'contributed significantly to regional dimensional stability research' was the most creative of them.

title: Warioland Full Membership Application
description:
Warioland's second application for full Congress membership. The first application, submitted during the founding session observer period and formally logged in early 1026 BF, had been rejected in a preliminary committee review that never reached a floor vote — the territorial documentation Wario submitted included survey maps that three separate cartographers identified as inconsistent with actual geographical features of the Warioland region, two deeds of territorial sovereignty that bore forged authentication seals from the Diamond City municipal authority, and a population census whose methodology section described procedures that, if actually followed, would have counted several residents multiple times and excluded the underground mining communities entirely. The committee review was conducted by the Iron Hills Dwarven Holds delegate, who had extensive experience identifying fraudulent cartographic claims, and the Beanbean Kingdom's administrative secretariat. Their joint report was thirteen pages long and used the phrase 'procedurally irregular' seven times and 'demonstrably false' twice. The report was delivered to Wario's representative — who was, based on multiple witness accounts, Wario wearing a slightly different hat and a pair of glasses — in a closed session. The representative did not contest the findings. The application was withdrawn before a floor vote could occur, which meant the rejection was administrative rather than legislative and Warioland could reapply without a formal denial on record. This was, as Waluigi noted at the time, the most competent thing the first application achieved.

The second application, submitted fourteen months later, was substantially different. The territorial documentation included certified survey reports from two independent cartographic firms, neither of which had prior commercial relationships with Warioland. The population census had been conducted by the Beanbean Kingdom's administrative office under contract — Queen Bean had agreed to this arrangement after a private conversation with Wario whose contents have never been disclosed, though Queen Bean later described the meeting as 'productive in the sense that productive means something eventually resulted from it.' The population count was lower than Wario's original self-reported figures by approximately 30%, which suggested the original figures had been inflated, but was internally consistent and independently verified. The Diamond City municipal authority provided a notarized statement clarifying that they had not issued the authentication seals on the first application's documents and that the seals were forgeries, a statement they provided voluntarily and that Mayor of Diamond City described as 'closing a procedural loop we should have addressed when it opened.'

The substantive objection to the second application came from the Pokémon League's Champion Alder, who submitted a seventeen-page brief documenting labor conditions in Warioland's mining operations. The brief identified nine specific practices that the Pokémon League argued violated the Species Recognition Compact passed at the founding session, including evidence that Wario employed workers in conditions that did not meet the compact's minimum standards for recognized sapient species, that worker complaints had no formal resolution mechanism, and that at least three distinct sapient species employed in the mines had not been formally recognized by Warioland's domestic legal framework. The brief was formally entered into the session record. Alder's delegate read portions of it aloud. Toadsworth the Elder supported the objection and noted that Warioland's compliance record with existing observer obligations had been 'inconsistent at best.' Several Non-Aligned delegates expressed sympathy for the objection without committing to a no vote. The Iron Hills Dwarven Holds, who had conducted the first application's fraud review, stated that the second application's documentation met procedural standards and that documentation compliance was the appropriate threshold for membership consideration, not labor practices that were subject to ongoing bilateral review. This argument — that meeting the paperwork standard was sufficient for admission even if behavioral standards were not yet met — carried the day.
aftermath: Wario attended the admission ceremony in person. He arrived forty minutes late, ate the majority of the ceremonial catering before most delegates had served themselves, and delivered an eight-minute speech that was primarily about himself — specifically about his personal business acumen, his vision for Warioland's economic growth, and his certainty that the Congress would benefit from his membership in ways he declined to specify. He referred to the Congress as 'this organization' throughout rather than by name, which may have been contemptuous or may have reflected genuine unfamiliarity with the institution he had just joined. He shook hands with Queen Bean and called her 'Bean Lady' which she accepted without visible reaction. He did not acknowledge the Pokémon League's delegate or Toadsworth the Elder, both of whom had voted against his admission. He acknowledged Waluigi across the room with a nod that several observers described as the most genuine moment of the ceremony. Compliance with the Species Recognition Compact's labor provisions has been reviewed twice since admission. The first review found 'meaningful progress with significant gaps remaining.' The second review found 'similar progress at a similar rate,' which is a diplomatic way of saying the situation had not materially changed. The workers in question remain employed. Their conditions remain subject to ongoing review. The review process continues.
waluigiComment:
Waluigi voted yes. Waluigi raised his hand. The hand did not count because the hand never counts. Waluigi is noting for the record that the hand was raised and the intention was yes.

Wario is not a good man. Waluigi has known Wario for a long time and has no illusions about what Wario is. Wario is greedy in a way that is almost architectural — it is not a personality trait, it is a structural feature of how he processes the world. Everything is measured in what it is worth to Wario. Everything. Including relationships. Including Waluigi. Waluigi knows this about Wario. Waluigi has always known this about Wario. Waluigi voted yes anyway.

Here is why. The Congress is better with Wario inside it than outside it. Wario controls real territory with a real population. That population deserves to have their nation represented at the table that makes decisions affecting them. Wario's workers — the ones the Pokémon League correctly identified as not being treated according to the standards the Congress set — those workers are better served by Warioland being a Congress member subject to Species Recognition Compact review than by Warioland being an outsider with no Congress obligations whatsoever. You cannot hold Wario to standards he has not agreed to. Membership is the mechanism by which he agreed. Waluigi voted yes because the mechanism matters even when the person agreeing to use it is doing so reluctantly and will comply minimally and needs to be watched.

Also, and Waluigi will say this plainly: Wario is the only person Waluigi has been genuinely glad to see walk into a room in the past fourteen years of attending these sessions. This is not an endorsement of Wario's governance. It is an acknowledgment that 'someone you are genuinely glad to see' and 'someone who governs well' are different categories and Waluigi is capable of holding both simultaneously.

The Pokémon League's objections were correct. The labor brief was accurate. The workers deserve better. Waluigi voted yes because Warioland being a member creates the possibility of demanding better. It does not guarantee it. Nothing guarantees it. But membership creates the lever. You cannot pull a lever that does not exist.

Wario ate most of the ceremonial catering. Waluigi had been looking forward to the catering. These two facts coexist with everything else Waluigi has written above.

title: Rakasha Clans Census Dispute Resolution
description: The Rakasha Clans, admitted as observers in the founding session batch and present through the Saddle Arabia sponsorship network, contested their population tier classification as Small. Their argument was methodological: the census procedures used to count populations for seat allocation assumed that people lived in fixed residences and could be counted there. The Rakasha Clans are nomadic. Their population moves seasonally across defined territories. When census takers arrived at Rakasha settlements, they found whoever happened to be present at that moment, counted them, and left. They did not follow the migration routes. They did not count populations at seasonal gathering sites. They did not use the Rakasha Clans' own internal census records, which documented family units and seasonal movement patterns and produced population estimates 40-60% higher than the external count. The Rakasha High Rakasha argued this was not a dispute about whether they had more people — they demonstrably did have more people — but about whether the Congress's census methodology was designed to produce accurate counts or convenient ones. Their formal request was for reclassification from Small to Medium population tier, which would increase their seat allocation and change their voting weight in future sessions.

notable_nay: several nations with nomadic minority populations they did not want recounted

aftermath: Failed on a bloc vote by nearly every nation that had populations counted by the same methodology. The logic was explicit if unspoken: if the Rakasha Clans' methodology complaint was upheld, the same argument applied to nomadic and semi-nomadic populations in at least eleven other member territories. Seat allocations would shift. Current seat holders voted to protect current seat allocations. The Rakasha Clans' complaint was legitimate. The methodology is still broken. The Iron Hills delegate — who had done the most to develop the original census standards — voted no with visible discomfort and submitted a written statement explaining that his vote was not an endorsement of the methodology but a recognition that reopening population counts at the first session after founding would destabilize the entire seat allocation framework. He recommended a formal methodology review to be conducted by 1030 BF. The methodology review was never scheduled. Four other nations with mobile or dispersed populations — the Dry Dry Kingdom, the Rakasha Clans themselves in a different context, Yoshi Clans Coalition, and one founding member that requested anonymity — have since had census undercounting documented but have not formally raised the issue because they watched what happened at this session.
waluigiComment: The nations who voted no were not wrong that changing the methodology would affect their own census numbers. They were wrong about why that was a reason to vote no. The purpose of a census is to count people accurately. If your methodology undercounts people, the correct response is to fix the methodology, not to protect the undercount because the accurate number would disadvantage you. This is not a complicated principle. The Congress understood it and voted against it anyway because accurate numbers and convenient numbers are different things and the Congress, when forced to choose, generally prefers the convenient ones. The Rakasha High Rakasha gave a speech that was the most precise summary of institutional self-interest that Waluigi has heard in fourteen years of attending these sessions. He said: you do not have an accurate census methodology; you have a methodology that produces numbers you find acceptable. He was correct. He lost. He came back in 1035 with a coalition and a narrower ask and won something smaller but real. Waluigi has taken notes on this approach. Waluigi has recommended it to other delegations. It works more often than immediately asking for everything. It does not work as fast as immediately asking for everything would, if the Congress were the kind of institution that rewarded it. The Congress is not that kind of institution.

title: Mordor Membership Application
description:
The most contentious membership vote in Congress history, argued across three separate sessions spanning six weeks. The Land of Mordor's application was submitted by The Mouth of Sauron's Successor — a diplomatic representative whose credentials were legitimate under Mordor's governance structure even though no Congress member had prior diplomatic relations with Mordor and several had active historical grievances. The application argued that Mordor controlled defined sovereign territory, maintained a stable (if unconventional) governance structure, had a population that fell within established membership tiers, and that the Congress's founding principle of universal representation meant a Congress without Mordor was a Congress that had decided some nations did not deserve to be at the table.

The opposition was extensive. Gondor's ambassador, whose nation had the most direct historical conflict with Mordor, submitted a formal objection arguing that Mordor's governance did not include any civilian oversight mechanism, that its history of aggressive expansion constituted an ongoing threat to regional stability, and that admitting Mordor was not the same as recognizing a nation — it was providing institutional legitimacy to an actor that had historically operated outside all institutional frameworks. The Elves of Lindon submitted a separate written objection. The Pokémon League raised concerns about Mordor's compliance with Species Recognition Compact standards given documented treatment of populations within its territory. The Mages Guild observer delegation provided technical analysis of Mordor's magical infrastructure and its implications for dimensional monitoring.

The debate produced what became known as the Mordor Compromise: a set of enhanced monitoring provisions specifically applied to members 'whose governance structures do not include recognized civilian oversight mechanisms.' These provisions included mandatory quarterly reporting to a standing oversight committee, enhanced observer access to territory for compliance verification, and a five-year probationary period before full voting rights on military cooperation resolutions would be granted. The provisions were written in language general enough to apply theoretically to any qualifying member, but the qualifying criteria were defined specifically enough that only Mordor met them. This legal architecture was intentional. It allowed the Congress to claim it had established universal standards while creating standards that were, functionally, Mordor-specific.

Gondor voted no through all three sessions. The Elves of Lindon voted no. The Pokémon League's delegate changed their vote between the second and third sessions after the monitoring provisions were strengthened, a reversal that was politically significant but not sufficient to overcome the underlying concern. The Progressive Bloc fractured: Beanbean Kingdom ultimately voted yes, reasoning that Mordor inside the Congress with enhanced monitoring was preferable to Mordor outside any framework. The vote passed on the third session by eight votes over the two-thirds threshold.

notable_yea: Koopa Troop (observer, no vote but expressed support)
notable_abstain: Pokémon League Regions (third session — changed to yes after provisions strengthened)

aftermath: The Congress's greatest achievement and most significant failure simultaneously. Greatest because it established that membership requires minimum governance standards and that the Congress would define and apply those standards even for applicants with significant opposition. Failure because the minimum standards were written to accommodate the worst applicant rather than to reflect genuine baseline requirements. The Mordor monitoring provisions have been reviewed four times since 1031. Mordor has complied with the reporting requirements on two of those reviews and submitted incomplete reports on the other two. The oversight committee has accepted the incomplete reports rather than escalating to formal noncompliance proceedings. The five-year probationary period for military cooperation voting ended in 1036. Mordor has voted on three military cooperation resolutions since then. The circular table arrangement created so no delegation was technically adjacent to Mordor while all were technically equal is still in use. It was designed as a compromise. It became permanent.
waluigiComment:
The Mordor Compromise is a document that says: we have established minimum standards, and we have written those standards to ensure that the entity we are most concerned about meets them. Read it carefully and this is obvious. Waluigi read it carefully. Waluigi said so in session. Waluigi was told that the standards were general and applied to all members equally. Waluigi pointed out that no other current or prospective member met the criteria that triggered the enhanced provisions. The session moved to the next item.

Waluigi voted yes. Waluigi will explain this clearly: Mordor exists. Mordor controls territory. Mordor has a population. That population is served by Mordor having international obligations, even obligations that Mordor will comply with minimally and reluctantly and incompletely. The alternative — refusing membership and leaving Mordor outside any international framework — does not make Mordor less dangerous. It makes Mordor less accountable. These are different things. Waluigi voted yes because accountability, however minimal, is better than none.

Gondor's vote no was also correct. Both of these things are true simultaneously. Gondor was right that the monitoring provisions were written to accommodate rather than constrain. Waluigi was right that accommodation within a framework is better than no framework. The Congress could only process one position. It chose Waluigi's, for Gondor's reasons. The compromise that resulted from Gondor's refusal to stop objecting is the only reason the enhanced monitoring provisions exist at all. If Gondor had not made noise, the provisions would have been weaker. If Waluigi had not voted yes, the provisions might not have passed. Both contributions mattered. Neither delegation will describe it this way.

title: Cybernetic Collectives Full Membership Application
description: Application from the Cybernetic Collectives — a distributed network of augmented persons and fully synthetic intelligences claiming sovereign digital and physical territory across seventeen member nation territories — for transition from observer to full membership status. The application raised philosophical questions that had not been fully resolved by the Internet Federation's founding admission: the Federation was a digital governance structure that controlled infrastructure. The Collectives were people. Distributed people. People who existed in multiple locations simultaneously, who had governance structures that operated across jurisdictions, and whose population count varied depending on whether you counted each instance of a synthetic consciousness separately or each individual consciousness regardless of how many instances it ran. The application included what the Collectives described as the most precise documentation of distributed sovereignty ever submitted to an international body. It was 847 pages long. The Internet Federation's Digital Plenipotentiary sponsored the application and argued that the Internet Federation precedent settled the core question. The Regal Empire argued that the precedent applied to infrastructure governance, not personhood, and that the Collectives' distributed existence across member territories constituted something closer to immigration than sovereignty. Several smaller nations noted that they had not been consulted about Collective members residing within their territories and were uncomfortable discovering they had hosted a sovereign entity without realizing it.
aftermath: Controversial but ultimately followed the Internet Federation precedent. The Cybernetic Collectives are the second-smallest delegation by seat count — their population-tier classification was contested because population counting for distributed synthetic consciousness remains methodologically unresolved — but have more data processing capacity than the rest of the Congress combined. They have used this capacity to produce comprehensive policy analysis on seventeen resolutions since admission, all of which have been technically accurate and none of which have been politically comfortable for the nations being analyzed. Their session reports are the most read and least cited documents in Congress history. Several members find the Collectives' analytical capabilities unsettling. Two have formally requested that Collective members not analyze their domestic policies. Both requests were declined on grounds that publicly available information is publicly available.
waluigiComment:
The Cybernetic Collectives delegate opened their admission statement by speaking simultaneously in 847 languages. Every delegate who had a translation device received it in their preferred language. Delegates without translation devices received it in whatever language their neighbor was hearing. Waluigi was in the room. Waluigi will not pretend it was not impressive. Waluigi will also not pretend it was not slightly threatening, in the way that any demonstration of capability significantly exceeding your own is threatening even when the demonstrator means no harm.

Waluigi voted yes. The Species Recognition Compact that Waluigi helped defend at this very Congress established that sapience is sapience. The Cybernetic Collectives are sapient. Their governance structure is unusual. Their existence is distributed in ways that make traditional sovereignty concepts awkward. None of these are arguments for exclusion — they are arguments for developing better frameworks, which the Congress has consistently failed to do because developing better frameworks requires admitting that existing frameworks are inadequate, and institutions resist this admission.

The fifteen nations who voted no were voting for the comfort of existing categories over the accuracy of recognizing what was actually in front of them. Waluigi has sympathy for this impulse. Categories exist because they are useful. They become problematic when maintaining them requires ignoring reality. Reality in 1031 BF included distributed synthetic sapient beings who controlled sovereign territory and had governance structures. The Congress could acknowledge this or it could not. Waluigi voted to acknowledge it.

The Collectives have since analyzed seventeen resolutions. Their analysis of vote_012 — the Rakasha census dispute — was the most precise demolition of a failed institutional decision Waluigi has ever read. The Congress did not formally respond to it. The analysis is in the archive. It will be relevant in 1133 BF when seat allocations are unfrozen.

title: Mages Guild Full Membership Application
description:
Application from the Mages Guild for full voting membership. The Guild's argument was that their cross-border mandate, unique expertise, and practical contribution to Congress operations since 1026 constituted a form of functional sovereignty even without exclusive territorial control. The Archmage's Delegate presented documentation of Guild operations across forty-three member territories, all conducted with member consent, none of which had generated territorial disputes because the Guild's operations were technical rather than political. The counter-argument, most forcefully made by Gondor's ambassador, was that functional contribution did not create sovereignty and that allowing expertise-based membership would open the door to applications from any sufficiently useful organization, potentially including the Freelancer Underworld if they became sufficiently useful to enough members. The Pokémon League supported the application. Beanbean Kingdom supported the application. The Regal Empire, which had been quietly uncomfortable with the Mages Guild's analytical support for dimensional monitoring since 1026, did not support the application and applied back-channel pressure through the Iron Pact.

The vote on the third day of the session was 18-19-4. The application failed by one vote. The nation whose delegate was absent — attending a bilateral meeting that had been requested by the Regal Empire's Imperial Chancellor's office the previous day and scheduled at a time that overlapped with the Mages Guild vote — has cycled through three different delegates since 1031. None of them have been informed of the scheduling conflict. The Archmage's Delegate did not request a delay to the vote when the absence was noted, stating that the Guild would not win a membership application by procedural maneuver. The Guild has not reapplied.

notable_yea: Iron Hills Dwarven Holds (scientific community relationships)
notable_nay: several Non-Aligned members under economic pressure
notable_abstain: one member (absent due to scheduling conflict — see description)

aftermath: Failed by one vote under circumstances that were either coincidental or were not. The Mages Guild has not formally accused anyone of engineering the scheduling conflict. They have noted, in their annual advisory report to the Congress, that the advisory body with the most dimensional monitoring expertise has the least formal authority in the Congress that most needs dimensional monitoring expertise. This observation has been included in every annual report since 1031. It is now the ninth year the observation has been included. The Congress has not formally responded to it. The Raventree Fracture emergency response team requested Mages Guild technical assistance within six hours of the fracture event. The Guild provided it without conditions, without asking for formal authority, and without noting that this was the ninth year they had been providing essential assistance without formal authority. The Archmage's Delegate's expression during the 1040 emergency session has been previously described. It has not improved with documentation.
waluigiComment:
One vote. One delegate, absent because a meeting was scheduled by someone with an interest in that delegate being elsewhere, at the exact time the vote occurred. Waluigi does not have proof that this was deliberate. Waluigi has the sequence of events, the party that requested the meeting, the timing of the scheduling, and fourteen years of watching how the Regal Empire operates when it wants something to fail quietly. The sequence is suggestive. The proof is absent. Waluigi is saving this observation.

The nation whose delegate missed the vote has had three different delegates since 1031. None of them know. Waluigi knows. Waluigi has not told them because telling them would require disclosing information Waluigi obtained through methods that are technically outside the bounds of official Congress procedure. Waluigi has been operating technically outside the bounds of official Congress procedure since 1026. The information exists. Waluigi is holding it.

The Mages Guild are the most useful body in the Congress. They have the most relevant expertise for the most serious problems the Congress faces. They have no formal authority. They have provided essential assistance without formal authority for fourteen years without complaint. The Archmage's Delegate is either a very good person or has calculated that patience is the correct long-term strategy or both. Waluigi suspects both. Waluigi respects it regardless.

When the Raventree Fracture happened and the Congress voted unanimously to authorize emergency response, the first people on the ground were Mages Guild staff who had been monitoring the situation informally since the monitoring committee was defunded in 1031. They were there before the authorization. They did not wait for the vote. They knew what was happening because they had been watching because watching was what they did whether or not they were paid to do it and whether or not they had formal authority to do it. Waluigi finds this more admirable than anything that has happened in the official session record in the past fourteen years. Waluigi voted yes in 1031. The hand did not count. The hand was right.

title: Dimensional Monitoring Committee Restructuring
description:
A Regal Empire proposal to restructure the Dimensional Barrier Monitoring Committee established under the founding resolution, citing jurisdictional overreach in the committee's monitoring activities over sovereign territories. The 'restructuring' as described in the proposal involved: eliminating the committee's standing staff and replacing them with a rotating voluntary roster of member-nation representatives; removing the mandatory reporting requirement and replacing it with optional self-reporting; transferring the committee's data archive to member-nation custody rather than a central repository; and reducing the committee's meeting frequency from quarterly to annually at minimum. In practice, these changes eliminated the committee's capacity to function as a monitoring body. A monitoring body run by voluntary rotating staff with no mandatory reporting and custody of its own data is not a monitoring body — it is a framework that can be pointed to when someone asks why there is no monitoring body.

The Regal Empire's stated justification was sovereignty: member nations had not consented to having their dimensional infrastructure observed by a standing international committee. The technical argument was that the founding resolution's consent provisions had been ambiguous and that the committee had been operating beyond its mandate. The Mages Guild's advisory submission — not a vote, an advisory submission, because the Guild does not vote — documented seventeen instances where the committee's monitoring had provided early warning data that member nations had acted on to prevent or mitigate dimensional incidents. The advisory submission noted that the committee's 1028 report had flagged anomalous readings in the Raventree region. The advisory submission was entered into the record. It was not discussed substantively before the vote.

The Beanbean Kingdom's Queen Bean requested a delay to allow full review of the Mages Guild submission. The request was denied on procedural grounds. The Progressive Bloc voted against the restructuring as a bloc. The Iron Pact voted for it as a bloc. The Sovereignty Bloc fractured: Gondor and the Iron Hills voted against; the Mushroom Kingdom, citing concerns about monitoring infrastructure over sovereign Mushroom Kingdom territory, voted for. The Mushroom Kingdom's vote was the decisive swing. With the Mushroom Kingdom's seats added to the Iron Pact bloc, the restructuring passed by two votes over the simple majority threshold.

notable_yea: several Non-Aligned members under Iron Pact economic pressure
notable_abstain: multiple Non-Aligned members who wanted neither to support the Empire nor oppose it publicly

aftermath: The committee that would have had fourteen years of dimensional barrier data by 1040 BF ceased to function within three months of the vote. The skeleton framework technically still exists — it meets once a year, attended by one voluntary representative from each member nation who wishes to participate, which is currently six nations. It produces no reports because it has no staff to produce them. Its data archive was distributed to member nations and has not been systematically maintained. The three reports it produced in its active years — 1026, 1027, and 1028 — survived in Mages Guild custody because the Guild made copies when the archive was being transferred. When the Raventree Fracture emergency response team assembled in 1040, their baseline data consisted of those three reports, fourteen years out of date, and whatever monitoring individual member nations had conducted on their own, which was inconsistent and incompatible. The response team is working blind in regions where fourteen years of trend data would have made the difference between responding to a crisis and preventing it. Toadsworth the Elder, whose Mushroom Kingdom vote provided the margin of passage, has not publicly commented on this resolution since 1031.
waluigiComment:
847 resolutions since the Congress was founded. This is the one that will kill people. This is the one that already has. Waluigi raised this issue in 1026 when the monitoring resolution passed. Waluigi raised it again in 1031 when the monitoring committee produced its third report noting anomalies in the Raventree region. Waluigi raised it when the restructuring was proposed. Waluigi's hand did not count in 1026. Waluigi's hand did not count in 1031. The dimensional fracture does not care who is sitting and who is standing or whose hand is counted and whose is not.

The Mushroom Kingdom's vote was the margin. Waluigi will not pretend otherwise and will not soften it. Toadsworth the Elder is a careful and experienced diplomat who has served the Mushroom Kingdom with genuine competence for decades. He voted to eliminate the dimensional monitoring committee because the Regal Empire's framing of the issue as a sovereignty question was politically effective and because the Mushroom Kingdom was, at the time, navigating difficult relationships with multiple Iron Pact members and could not afford to be seen as opposing the Empire on a procedural matter that could be characterized as imperial overreach. This was a rational calculation. It was wrong. Both things are true.

Waluigi was present in 1031. Waluigi watched the vote happen. Waluigi had read the three monitoring reports. Waluigi had read the 1028 report's section on Raventree regional anomalies. Waluigi understood what the vote meant. Waluigi raised the hand that does not count. Waluigi is now watching the response teams operate without the data that would have existed if the hand that does not count had counted in this case.

Waluigi is not going to say I told you so. Waluigi is going to sit in the chamber while the unanimous emergency authorization vote congratulates itself on rapid response. Waluigi is going to sit very quietly and not say it very loudly. The people who voted for this restructuring are watching the Raventree response and understanding, each in their own way and at their own pace, what they voted for in 1031. Waluigi does not need to say it. Reality is saying it. Reality is thorough and does not care about parliamentary procedure either.

title: Koopa Troop Conditional Full Membership
description:
Application for full membership from the Koopa Troop, which had held observer status since the founding session. The application was the most procedurally complex in Congress history at the time of its submission: the Koopa Troop had an unresolved territorial dispute with the Mushroom Kingdom, which under Congress charter rules meant the Mushroom Kingdom was required to co-sponsor any Koopa Troop membership application as the party to the dispute. Toadsworth the Elder co-sponsored the application with an expression that several session attendees independently described as looking like he had swallowed something unpleasant. The Koopa Troop's delegate was Kamek, representing Bowser's interests, though Bowser himself attended the final session in person — an attendance that required rearranging the chamber seating to accommodate his physical dimensions, a logistical challenge that the session secretariat handled with professional speed and visible resignation.

The conditional provisions were the substantive content of the vote: the Koopa Troop's admission was conditioned on a formal renunciation of castle-seizure practices targeting member-nation infrastructure, an acknowledgment of Mushroom Kingdom territorial sovereignty over all territories currently recognized as Mushroom Kingdom sovereign, and a commitment to bilateral arbitration for any future territorial disputes rather than unilateral military action. The Koopa Troop's representative accepted all three conditions. The Koopa Troop's representative was Kamek. Kamek's acceptance of the conditions was legally binding. Bowser's expression during Kamek's acceptance speech was observed by fourteen delegates. Several of them took notes. The notes describe an expression that was not inconsistent with someone who found the conditions acceptable as a procedural matter and considered the question of implementation to be separate from the question of acceptance.

notable_yea: Mushroom Kingdom (sponsor, required, voted yes with visible discomfort)

aftermath: The Mushroom Kingdom's sponsorship is recorded. Toadsworth the Elder's vote is recorded. The Koopa Troop has since partially honored the conditions. The castle-seizure renunciation has been followed in the sense that no Mushroom Kingdom castles have been seized through the formal military campaign model that the renunciation described. Whether alternative methods of achieving similar outcomes constitute compliance with the renunciation's spirit is a question before bilateral arbitration that has been pending since 1035. The acknowledgment of Mushroom Kingdom territorial sovereignty has been honored in Congress sessions where Koopa Troop representatives have not contested Mushroom Kingdom territorial claims. It has been less honored in operational contexts. Bowser attended the admission ceremony, sat in a chair that was brought in specifically for the occasion, ate approximately forty percent of the ceremonial catering before most delegates had served themselves (catching up to Wario's founding-era record), and shook hands with Toadsworth the Elder in a manner that Toadsworth described afterward as 'a handshake.' Bowser called the Congress 'exactly what he expected it to be' without specifying whether this was a compliment.
waluigiComment:
Bowser sat in the front row. Not the chair arranged for him — the chair was in the second row behind the membership applicant position. Bowser sat in the front row in a chair that was technically designated for the Mushroom Kingdom delegation. Toadsworth was sitting in that chair. Toadsworth moved. This is not in the official session minutes but it happened. Waluigi was there.

Waluigi voted yes. The Koopa Troop controls extensive territory, has a large population, and has been an observer since the founding session with genuine engagement in several Congress processes despite the obvious political awkwardness of their relationship with the Mushroom Kingdom. Excluding them from membership because their relationship with the Mushroom Kingdom is complicated is not a principled position — it is using the Congress's membership criteria as a weapon in a bilateral dispute, which is exactly the kind of thing the Congress exists to prevent.

The conditions were appropriate. Whether they will be honored appropriately is a different question and the answer so far is 'partially, in a way that satisfies the letter more than the spirit.' This is also Wario's compliance model. Waluigi is beginning to think that 'partially, with visible reluctance, in ways that satisfy the letter more than the spirit' is the best outcome available for nations whose compliance requires ongoing political will rather than simple administrative follow-through.

Waluigi has complicated feelings about Bowser. Mostly competitive ones. Bowser and Waluigi have never had a direct competition of any kind that Waluigi has won. Waluigi has not stopped trying. This is relevant context for understanding why Waluigi's feelings about Bowser's Congress membership are complicated in ways that go beyond the policy questions. Waluigi voted on the policy question. The other feelings are Waluigi's private business and will remain so.

title: Iron Legion Full Membership Application
proposedBy: Iron Pact (joint: Regal Empire, Iron Hills faction delegates)
description:
Application for the Iron Legion to transition from its founding-session observer status to full voting membership. The application was sponsored by the Iron Pact and argued that the Iron Legion controlled defined territorial installations across seventeen regions, maintained stable governance through its command structure, had a population of personnel and dependents exceeding several current member nations' population tiers, and had been a constructive observer participant in Congress proceedings since 1026. The counter-argument, led by the Pokémon League's delegate and supported by Beanbean Kingdom, was structural: the Iron Legion is a military organization. It has no civilian population in the traditional sense. Its governance is command hierarchy, not civilian government. Admitting the Iron Legion was not analogous to admitting Mordor, which at least had a civilian-adjacent administrative structure and a population that included non-military persons. Admitting the Iron Legion was admitting that the Congress would grant full voting rights to a military command structure with no civilian oversight and no civilian population.

The Iron Pact's lobbying before the session was extensive. The Regal Empire's Imperial Chancellor held bilateral meetings with sixteen delegations in the ten days before the vote. The Iron Hills faction delegates — a minority within the Iron Hills delegation that had developed closer ties to the Regal Empire than the Hold's primary position — had been building relationships with Non-Aligned bloc members for three sessions. The Sovereignty Bloc fractured badly: Gondor voted no, the Rohirrim voted no, the Shire voted no, but the Iron Hills as a delegation voted yes over its primary delegate's stated objection, a result that reflected the faction dynamics and was challenged as a procedural irregularity before being ruled procedurally valid by the session chair. The Progressive Bloc was the only bloc that held: every Progressive Bloc member voted no or abstained.

notable_yea: several Non-Aligned members under economic pressure

aftermath: The most alarming membership vote since Mordor, and in some ways more alarming, because the Mordor Compromise established enhanced monitoring provisions. The Iron Legion has full membership without enhanced monitoring provisions. Their seats are exercised by military officers whose titles are procedural aliases because the Iron Legion's actual command structure is not disclosed in Congress documentation. They have voted on seventeen resolutions since admission. Their voting record is notable for consistent support of resolutions expanding Congress security forces, consistent opposition to transparency measures, and consistent support for resolutions that create legal frameworks permitting cross-border military action under specified conditions. None of this is surprising. All of it is documented. The precedent for future applications from armed non-state actors has not been formally discussed by the Congress. The Iron Legion's delegate shook Waluigi's hand after the vote. The handshake was the kind of handshake that communicates something without words. Waluigi understood the communication. Waluigi has not discussed it publicly.
waluigiComment:
The Congress admitted a military without a country. Read that again slowly. A military. An armed command structure. Without a country. Without a civilian population. Without civilian oversight. With full voting rights on resolutions that affect civilian populations across all member nations.

Waluigi was present for the Iron Legion's founding-session observer admission in 1026. Waluigi noted that the unanimous vote was suspicious. Waluigi was correct that it was suspicious. Ten years of watching the Iron Legion build relationships, provide services, create dependencies, and position itself for exactly this moment — Waluigi watched all of it. Waluigi raised the pattern in sessions four times between 1026 and 1036. Waluigi's hand does not count. The pattern continued.

Waluigi objected formally during the debate. Waluigi's objection was entered into the session record as a comment from an unofficial attendee. The Iron Legion's lobbyists had spent ten days ensuring that the delegates who might have swung the vote were otherwise occupied, economically pressured, or genuinely persuaded. The Iron Hills faction situation was not an accident. The faction delegates who broke from the Hold's primary position had been cultivated for three sessions. Waluigi watched them being cultivated. Waluigi noted it in the sessions. Waluigi's notes are in the record. Nobody has asked Waluigi about the notes.

After the vote, the Iron Legion delegate found Waluigi in the corridor. The handshake was not hostile. It was something more uncomfortable than hostile. It was the kind of handshake that says: we know you know, and we know it doesn't matter, and we want you to know we know that. Waluigi shook the hand because refusing would have communicated more than Waluigi wanted to communicate. Waluigi then went home and wrote down everything he remembered about the handshake and everything he had documented about the Iron Legion's membership campaign. The document exists. Waluigi is saving it.

title: Raventree Fracture Emergency Response Authorization
proposedBy: Mages Guild (observer advisory) / multiple member sponsors
description: Emergency authorization for cross-border coordinated response to the Raventree Fracture dimensional event — the largest dimensional stability failure since the Chaos Heart Crisis, which the Congress was founded in the aftermath of. The authorization included: temporary suspension of standard border crossing protocols for authorized response teams; authorization for Mages Guild personnel to operate across all member territories without bilateral approval for the duration of the emergency; emergency reallocation of the Congressional Security Fund for response coordination; and establishment of a Joint Crisis Command with rotating member representation. The Mages Guild advisory submission accompanying the authorization request was the most technically comprehensive emergency brief in Congress history — and was also, as the Guild's Archmage Delegate noted in her spoken remarks, working entirely from baseline data that was fourteen years out of date because the monitoring committee had been defunded in 1031. She said this once, quietly, without elaboration, and moved immediately to the technical content. Most delegates heard it. The session moved forward without comment on it. The vote was called immediately, which was the appropriate thing to do given the urgency. The unanimous effective result — forty yes votes, two abstentions from nations with travel restrictions that prevented delegate participation, zero no votes — was achieved faster than any previous emergency authorization. Waluigi's unofficial observer chair in the back of the chamber was empty for the first time since the founding session. Several delegates noticed. One of them — the Beanbean Kingdom's Queen Bean — looked at the empty chair before casting her vote. She has not commented on why.

notable_yea: All present member delegations including Iron Pact, Sovereignty Bloc, Progressive Bloc, Non-Aligned
notable_abstain: Two member nations with travel or communication restrictions preventing delegate attendance — not opposition abstentions
notable_absent: Waluigi (unofficial observer) — first absence since founding session. Location: Raventree Manor fracture zone.

aftermath: Unanimous effective vote achieved in the fastest session in Congress history at forty-three minutes from call to close. Speed and unanimity cannot substitute for the fourteen years of dimensional monitoring baseline data the Congress chose to eliminate in vote_022 of 1031. The Mages Guild response teams had been monitoring the Raventree region informally since the monitoring committee was defunded, using Guild resources rather than Congress resources, because the Archmage had read the 1028 report's Raventree anomaly section and had decided someone should keep watching even without formal authority. This informal monitoring — underfunded, understaffed, and technically outside any authorized framework — is the only reason the response teams had any baseline data at all. The Archmage has not claimed credit for this decision in public. The session record credits the Mages Guild with 'providing essential advisory support.' The actual story is more specific than that and more damning to the Congress's 1031 decision than the session record indicates. The session minutes note Waluigi's absence as an unofficial observation — his attendance is not formally tracked because he is not formally a member of anything, but fourteen years of continuous presence makes an absence conspicuous even when the presence was never officially acknowledged. The session secretary recorded it as a footnote. It is the only footnote in the emergency session record.
waluigiComment:
Waluigi was not in the chamber.

In fourteen years of attending every session of the Glazed Congress — from the founding session that Waluigi reached on a borrowed train ticket to the most recent procedural session that three delegates bothered to attend — Waluigi has not missed a single one. Waluigi has sat in the back of the chamber in the chair that nobody assigned because nobody can assign a chair to an unofficial observer who does not technically exist in the attendance records. Waluigi has raised the hand that does not count on 847 resolutions. Waluigi has been there.

Waluigi was not there for vote 193.

Waluigi was at Raventree Manor. Waluigi was standing inside the dimensional fracture that the Congress was voting to respond to. While forty delegates raised their hands unanimously in the fastest session in Congress history, Waluigi was watching the walls of a building decide to become a different building in a different dimension. The ground was not the ground. The sky was not the sky. The mirrors were doing things that Waluigi will describe in a formal report when Waluigi has time to write a formal report and has stopped seeing the things the mirrors were doing when Waluigi closes his eyes.

Waluigi learned about the vote afterward. Someone — Waluigi does not know who — left a copy of the session minutes in the Raventree response coordination tent. The session was forty-three minutes. Unanimous. The authorization Waluigi has been arguing for since 1026 — cross-border dimensional response capability, Mages Guild operational authority, emergency coordination — passed without a single no vote on the day Waluigi was not present to see it.

The hand that does not count was not raised for the one vote it would have been proudest to be raised for. Waluigi is processing this.

The Archmage said the baseline data was fourteen years out of date. Waluigi knows this. Waluigi is standing in the consequence of this. The response teams are working blind in corridors where the physics change between steps. They are doing extraordinary work with inadequate information. The inadequate information is a choice the Congress made in 1031. Waluigi raised the hand that does not count on that vote too. The hand did not count. The dimensional fracture does not care.

Waluigi is told that Queen Bean looked at the empty chair before voting. Waluigi does not know how to feel about this. Waluigi has sat in that chair for fourteen years and never been certain that anyone noticed. Apparently someone noticed when the chair was empty. Waluigi is going to think about this for a while. Not now. Now Waluigi has work to do. The fracture does not wait for feelings.

Waluigi will be back for the next session. The chair will not be empty again. Waluigi has things to report that the Congress needs to hear from someone who was inside the fracture rather than voting about it from a comfortable chamber. The hand that does not count has fourteen years of not counting and one session of absence and Waluigi intends for the absence to be the more memorable of the two.

WAH. But quietly. There are wounded people nearby and Waluigi has priorities.

title: Iron Mandate Condemnation Resolution
proposedBy: Seven member nations (joint): Beanbean Kingdom, Pokémon League Regions, Yoshi's Island, Sarasaland, Flipside-Flopside, Pi'illo Kingdom, Elves of Lindon
description:
A formal condemnation resolution challenging the Regal Empire's Iron Mandate legislation, which granted the Iron Legion emergency domestic powers and included provisions that the seven sponsoring nations argued directly violated the Species Recognition Compact through supernatural persecution clauses. The Iron Mandate had been passed by the Regal Empire's domestic legislature three months prior. Its provisions allowed the Iron Legion to detain, relocate, and restrict the movements of persons classified as presenting 'supernatural risk profiles' — a classification the sponsoring nations argued was designed to target specific sapient species and cultural communities under a bureaucratic framework that did not require individual findings of wrongdoing. The Mages Guild advisory submission on the Iron Mandate's compliance with the Species Recognition Compact was forty-seven pages and concluded that six specific provisions were incompatible with the compact's core requirements.

The seven sponsoring nations had the votes to pass the condemnation. This was known before the session. What was also known before the session was that the Iron Pact — led by the Regal Empire — had made explicit to Non-Aligned bloc members and smaller Sovereignty Bloc nations that treating the condemnation as a legitimate Congress action would be treated as a hostile act against a founding member. The economic dependencies involved were not abstract: the Regal Empire controls significant trade infrastructure that smaller member nations depend on, and several delegates who would have voted yes on the condemnation had received private communications from their economic ministries documenting what a deteriorated relationship with the Empire would mean for their fiscal year. The vote date has not been scheduled. The seven sponsoring nations have not withdrawn the resolution. The Iron Legion continues to operate under the Iron Mandate's provisions. The independent observer investigation authorized in vote_045 has named its team members. The Regal Empire has not blocked them. Yet.

projected_nay_or_abstain_under_pressure: several Non-Aligned nations under economic pressure from Empire trade relationships

aftermath: Resolution pending. The seven sponsoring nations have the votes if every projected yes delegate attends and votes yes. Whether every projected yes delegate will attend and vote yes is a question about courage rather than arithmetic. The Regal Empire has made clear that passage would be treated as a hostile act. This threat is real — several nations have received specific economic communication from Imperial trade offices. Whether those nations will be moved more by economic pressure or by the content of the Mages Guild's forty-seven page compliance analysis is the question the Congress has not yet answered. The Iron Mandate continues to operate. The people affected by it continue to be affected. The vote date has not been set.
waluigiComment:
The Congress has the votes. The Congress does not have the courage. These are different things and Waluigi has been watching the gap between them widen across fourteen years of sessions.

Waluigi knows which delegates are afraid. Waluigi knows which ones have received communications from Imperial trade offices. Waluigi knows which ones would vote yes if the vote were secret and which ones are calculating the cost of their yes vote against their next trade agreement renewal. Waluigi knows this because Waluigi has been in this chamber since 1026 counting things, including the votes of people who do not realize they are being counted by someone who has no seat and whose hand does not count.

The Species Recognition Compact is vote_003. Waluigi defended it then. Waluigi has defended it three times in procedural contexts since then. The Iron Mandate violates six specific provisions of the compact according to the most qualified technical body in the Congress. This is not ambiguous. This is not a close call. This is the Congress being asked to enforce its own founding document against a founding member that has decided its domestic interests outweigh its international obligations.

If this condemnation fails — not because the votes were not there, but because the delegates who had the votes could not summon the will to cast them — Waluigi does not know what the Congress is for. Waluigi has spent fourteen years believing the Congress is for something. Waluigi has defended this belief against considerable evidence. Vote 200 is the test Waluigi has been waiting for since 1026.

Waluigi will raise the hand that does not count. Waluigi will be in the chamber. Waluigi will be watching every delegate who has the vote and does not cast it, and Waluigi will know why they did not cast it, and Waluigi will remember. Waluigi has always remembered. The records exist because Waluigi has been maintaining them from a borrowed chair in the back of the chamber since before the first session gaveled in.

The people affected by the Iron Mandate are not waiting for the vote date to be scheduled. They are living inside the Mandate right now. The Congress's courage or lack of it is not an abstract institutional question. It is a specific practical fact that affects specific people's lives. Waluigi has the list of those people. Waluigi does not share the list. But Waluigi knows every name on it, the same way Waluigi knows every name on the vote_003 list. The lists are connected. They were always connected. The Congress will decide whether they remain connected or whether the 1026 promise was a fourteen-year temporary arrangement.

WAH.
